identity.title: Dullness to percussion with decreased tactile fremitus (focal; conventional vs auscultatory percussion)

technique.how: With the patient sitting, percuss the posterior and lateral chest from apex to base comparing mirror-image sites; note any area where the note becomes dull or flat. At the same levels ask the patient to say 'ninety-nine' while palpating with the ulnar border of the hand to compare tactile fremitus side to side.
technique.prerequisites: Patient able to sit forward; bare skin; quiet environment.

interpretation.positive_finding: A focal area of dull or stony-dull percussion, typically basal, with reduced tactile fremitus over the same area (effusion) or increased fremitus (consolidation).
interpretation.negative_finding: Resonant, symmetric percussion note with symmetric fremitus; absence of reduced fremitus makes pleural effusion less likely (LR- about 0.2).
interpretation.pitfalls: Small effusions (<300-500 mL) and effusions in supine patients are missed; obesity, muscular chest wall and elevated hemidiaphragm can mimic basal dullness. Fremitus is unreliable in patients with weak voices or on positive-pressure ventilation.
interpretation.changes_what: Focal dullness: obtain CXR or lung POCUS to confirm effusion vs consolidation; normal fremitus and percussion in low-pretest patients may make imaging unnecessary.

estimates.population: Adults with respiratory symptoms in prospective diagnostic studies (5 studies, N=934)
estimates.quote: dullness to conventional percussion was most accurate for diagnosing pleural effusion (summary positive likelihood ratio, 8.7; 95% confidence interval, 2.2-33.8)

estimates.population: Adults with respiratory symptoms in prospective diagnostic studies (5 studies, N=934)
estimates.quote: the absence of reduced tactile vocal fremitus made pleural effusion less likely (negative likelihood ratio, 0.21; 95% confidence interval, 0.12-0.37)

estimates.population: Adults with clinically suspected pneumonia or acute cough; 17 prospective cohorts (9 primary care, 7 ED); CAP prevalence 10% primary care, 20% ED

sources.citation: Wong CL, Holroyd-Leduc J, Straus SE. Does this patient have a pleural effusion? JAMA. 2009;301(3):309-317.
Ebell MH, Chupp H, Cai X, Bentivegna M, Kearney M. Accuracy of signs and symptoms for the diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia: a meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2020;27(7):541-553.
Kalantri S, Joshi R, Lokhande T, et al. Accuracy and reliability of physical signs in the diagnosis of pleural effusion. Respir Med. 2007;101(3):431-438.
Metlay JP, Kapoor WN, Fine MJ. Does this patient have community-acquired pneumonia? Diagnosing pneumonia by history and physical examination. JAMA. 1997;278(17):1440-1445.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use a normal exam to exclude effusion in supine, ventilated or obese patients, or when pretest probability is high; image instead.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Dullness with fever and hypotension or with a rapidly enlarging effusion warrants urgent imaging and consideration of empyema or hemothorax.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Kalantri 2007 (Abstract): agreement between two blinded physicians was excellent for percussion note and vocal fremitus (kappa 0.84-0.89), good for auscultatory percussion (kappa 0.68-0.78).

extraction_notes: Pleural effusion LRs are the JAMA RCE summary estimates (Wong 2009) taken from the abstract; the RCE full text (with per-study sensitivity/specificity and auscultatory-percussion LRs) is not open access, so sens/spec and the auscultatory-percussion estimate are left null. Pneumonia LR+ for dullness is from Ebell 2020 abstract; LR- and sens/spec not reported in the abstract and full text is not open access. Kalantri 2007 abstract reports dull percussion as an independent predictor (OR 12.80, 95% CI 4.23-38.70) but its table-level LRs could not be viewed, so it is cited for reliability only.
